title: We are not Hindus
hookLine: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's book argued Sikhi was distinct, while honoring neighbors

lines: A TITLE LIKE A SLAMMED DOOR.
cards: A book title can sound like a slammed door. This one, in Punjabi, is Ham Hindu Nahin: we are not Hindus. Read only the cover and you might expect an attack.
Open it, and the author starts somewhere else. He's writing to his Hindu neighbors and friends with respect, he says, and he means them no ill will.
He simply wants to set down, plainly, from the Gurus' own words, what makes the Sikh path its own. The author is Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha.

teach.b: First, the question. In the years of the Singh Sabhas, a debate ran through the Punjab: were Sikhs a separate faith, or a branch of the wider Hindu family?
Some Hindu reformers held that Sikhs belonged within the Hindu fold, and some Sikhs agreed. Other Sikhs disagreed sharply. Second, the scholar.
Kahn Singh was a learned man from the princely state of Nabha, at home in Punjabi, Persian and the old texts.
He answered not with insults but with quotations, page after page, setting the Gurus' hymns beside the claim. Third, his evidence.
The Sikhs, he argued, have their own Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib; their own initiation, the Khalsa's amrit; their own rites for birth, marriage and death; their own places of worship.

And he pointed to the Gurus themselves, including a hymn you met some days ago: Guru Arjan, in Bhairo, saying he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and breath belong to the One whom some call Allah and some call Ram.
Kahn Singh read it as the Gurus marking out a path of their own. Fourth, the kindness. In the Punjab, some Sikh and Hindu families were kin, sharing weddings, festivals and grief.

teach.h: A LINE THAT DOESN'T PUSH AWAY.
teach.b: Kahn Singh's book draws a line around the Sikh path, but it doesn't push the neighbors away.
Hindus describe their own traditions in their own words; this lesson is about how one Sikh scholar said who his community was, while still sitting at a neighbor's table.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Ham Hindu Nahin as a scholar's case, built from the Gurus' hymns, that Sikhi is a distinct path, written with respect for Hindu neighbors.

games.q: you're Kahn Singh. a heated debate asks whether Sikhs are a separate faith. how do you answer?
o: set the Gurus' hymns beside the claim, with respect for neighbors.
games.why: he wrote Ham Hindu Nahin, a scholar's case built from quotations, opening with respect for Hindu friends.

practice: Finish this sentence quietly, in your own words: I am someone who… and let one honest answer come: a faith, a practice, a value, a place you belong.
Picture saying it to a neighbor who sees the world differently, with the same words but a warmer tone, and notice that the truth didn't change. If you pray, let Waheguru be the quiet you return to.

wordCard.voice: Kahn Singh, the scholar of Nabha who wrote Ham Hindu Nahin, setting out from the Gurus' words what makes Sikhi distinct, while honoring Hindu neighbors. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: distinct, and kind. A clear line, and an open door. Day nine hundred sixty-six, and the week closes.
